specAnchors.text: know the difference between mains electricity being alternating current (a.c.) and direct current (d.c.) being supplied by a cell or battery

primer.text: Two kinds of current power the world: the steady one-way flow from a battery, and the back-and-forth flow from the mains. This note defines direct and alternating current, contrasts their terminals, and pins down the UK mains figures — alternating current at 50 Hz and about 230 V — alongside the oscilloscope traces that tell them apart.

modules.title: Direct current from cells & batteries
modules.opening: A battery pushes charge the same way all the time: its positive and negative terminals never swap, so the current flows steadily one way around the circuit. That is direct current, and every cell or battery you have wired into a circuit produces it.
keyPoints: Direct current flows steadily one way round the circuit, positive to negative.
A d.c. supply keeps fixed positive and negative terminals.
Cells and batteries are the everyday sources of direct current.

low.restatement: Direct current goes one way only, from the positive terminal to the negative.
low.analogy: A one-way escalator: everyone moves in the same direction, all the time.
low.examPointer: All the circuits you have built so far are d.c. — the calculations you know already apply unchanged.

medium.restatement: The fixed polarity of the terminals is what fixes the direction: the current follows the potential difference, and that never reverses.
medium.analogy: A river bed that only ever slopes one way — the water has no choice of direction.
medium.examPointer: If asked for a source, say cells or batteries, not 'the plug'.

modules.title: Alternating current & the UK mains
modules.opening: The mains behaves differently: its two terminals keep trading polarity, so the current sweeps back and forth instead of holding one direction. That is alternating current. The frequency counts the sweeps each second — 50 of them in UK sockets — and the voltage sits near 230 V.
keyPoints: Alternating current changes direction continuously, moving back and forth.
An a.c. supply has two identical terminals whose polarity keeps swapping.
The frequency counts the back-and-forth direction changes each second.
UK mains delivers alternating current at 50 Hz and about 230 V.
Generators at power stations produce the mains alternating current.

low.restatement: Alternating current keeps reversing direction; UK mains does this 50 times a second at about 230 V.
low.analogy: A pendulum versus a one-way slide: the pendulum sweeps both ways, the slide only down.
low.examPointer: Learn the two mains numbers as a pair — 50 Hz and 230 V — questions rarely ask for one without the other.

medium.restatement: Because the terminals swap polarity continuously, neither is 'the positive one'; each is positive half the time and negative the other half.
medium.analogy: Two children on a see-saw taking turns being 'up' — neither holds the title for long.
medium.examPointer: Sketch the two oscilloscope traces: a flat line for d.c., an oscillating wave for a.c.

glossary.definition: A steady current flowing one way only, produced by cells and batteries.
A current that continuously changes direction, produced by generators and carried by the mains.
The number of back-and-forth direction changes per second, in hertz; UK mains is 50 Hz.
